question: When is a pretreatment biopsy not required?

options.B: When a thymic tumour is highly probable and upfront complete resection is achievable [IV, E]

correctAnswerText: When a thymic tumour is highly probable and upfront complete resection is achievable [IV, E]
explanation: Biopsy is not required if suspicion is high and upfront resection is achievable [IV, E]. In other situations a biopsy is required [IV, A]. Fine-needle aspiration is not recommended [IV, D] [1].
sourceArticle: SEOM-GECP-GETTHI clinical guidelines for the treatment of patients with thymic epithelial tumours (2021)

question: What is the relationship between thymoma and myasthenia gravis?

options.A: Every patient with thymoma has myasthenia
options.B: Antibody titre is the marker used to follow the tumour
options.C: Myasthenia occurs only with thymic carcinoma
options.D: Up to 30% of patients with thymoma have or develop myasthenia; 10–20% of patients with myasthenia have a thymoma

correctAnswerText: Up to 30% of patients with thymoma have or develop myasthenia; 10–20% of patients with myasthenia have a thymoma
explanation: Up to 30% of patients with thymoma present with or later develop myasthenia gravis, whereas 10–20% of patients with myasthenia have a thymoma. Acetylcholine-receptor antibodies remain positive and are not monitored as a tumour marker [1].
sourceArticle: SEOM-GECP-GETTHI clinical guidelines for the treatment of patients with thymic epithelial tumours (2021)

question: Standard surgery for a resectable tumour is:

options.C: Median sternotomy and, preferably, complete thymectomy including residual thymus and perithymic fat
options.D: Core biopsy and chemotherapy without an operation
options.E: Wedge resection of the lung only

correctAnswerText: Median sternotomy and, preferably, complete thymectomy including residual thymus and perithymic fat
explanation: If complete resection is achievable, surgery is the mainstay [IV, A]. Median sternotomy is the standard approach [IV, A]. Complete thymectomy is preferred [IV, B] [1].
sourceArticle: SEOM-GECP-GETTHI clinical guidelines for the treatment of patients with thymic epithelial tumours (2021)

question: Adjuvant chemotherapy after resection of a thymoma is:

options.A: Required for every stage I tumour
options.B: Given instead of radiotherapy for an R2 resection
options.C: The same recommendation as for every thymic carcinoma

explanation: There is no indication for adjuvant chemotherapy after R0 or R1 resection of thymoma [III, E]. Postoperative radiotherapy is a separate decision [1].
sourceArticle: SEOM-GECP-GETTHI clinical guidelines for the treatment of patients with thymic epithelial tumours (2021)

question: Postoperative radiotherapy is recommended for:

options.A: Stage III disease, thymic carcinoma, and R1 or R2 resection, at 45–50 Gy after complete resection and 56 Gy after R1
options.B: Stage I thymoma after R0 resection as a routine

correctAnswerText: Stage III disease, thymic carcinoma, and R1 or R2 resection, at 45–50 Gy after complete resection and 56 Gy after R1
explanation: Postoperative radiotherapy is recommended for stage III, thymic carcinoma, and R1 or R2 resection [IV, B]. The dose is 45–50 Gy after complete resection and 56 Gy after R1 [1].
sourceArticle: SEOM-GECP-GETTHI clinical guidelines for the treatment of patients with thymic epithelial tumours (2021)
